items.title: Your AI agent fixed the bug, but what else did it change?
items.summary: Today we’re publishing patching-bugs and regression-hunt, two plugins that let engineers delegate patch development and regression checks to agents. Our patching-bugs plugin reproduces reported bugs, develops fixes, and tests them. The regression-hunt plugin checks whether any changes break previously working and supported behavior. Engineers can direct the work and review their results; maintainers can supply their own security assumptions and patching requirements, so the agents work within the project’s rules.We built patching-bugs and regression-hunt through Patch the Planet, our joint initiative with OpenAI, where we’ve co-authored hundreds of security patches for widely used open-source projects. Motivated by our major successes on projects like Scapy, our plugins draw on our analysis of merged patches and thousands of our engineers’ Codex sessions.The plugins provide maintainers with a structured workflow, evidence, independent checks, and best practices to improve their patching hygiene. In our preliminary evaluations, regression-hunt produces 25% fewer false-positive findings than a baseline Codex agent prompted to “review the PR for regressions.”Standardizing the patching processOur September post reported regressions introduced by some of our Patch the Planet patches. Since then, we’ve reviewed every patch that a Trail of Bits engineer authored and maintainers merged upstream. The review confirmed 21 regressions from over 130 PRs merged: 16 functional, one performance, and four build/test (see appendix). None broke a security protection.(“Regression” refers to a new defect introduced by a change that breaks previously correct and supported behavior along a path a real user or attacker can reach.)For each patch, an agent looked for potential regressions, confirmed each one with a proof-of-concept (PoC) run before and after the change, and then passed the results to an engineer for review.The review was noisy: today’s bug disclosures arrive at an unprecedented speed and scale, and for patching to keep pace, the industry needs to increase its signal-to-noise ratio. The 21 confirmed regressions were identified among 58 candidates in a single run (~36% precision). But because agents take many different approaches and reach different results, each run generates more candidates to manually sort through.That led us to two conclusions:To introduce fewer regressions, we needed a standard way to write patches, with the same checks applied every time.To catch the regressions we still introduce, we needed a standard way to check for them, with written rules for what counts as a regression.Standardizing both steps also makes every run repeatable and comparable. No fixed checklist will catch every regression, so we collect agent trajectories from our engineers’ patching sessions, and use the tasks that an earlier version failed to benchmark for the next one (figure 1).Figure 1: Feedback loop for generating and evaluating patches. How we designed the pluginsWe used two primary sources to guide the design of our plugins: a review of every patch we merged upstream and the thousands of Codex sessions our engineers used to write those patches.This led to four principles that shaped our patching-bugs and regression-hunt plugins:Opinionated guidance in as few words as possible. We give the agent wide latitude and record only Trail of Bits’ judgment of what constitutes a good patch and a real regression. The goal is to direct the agent towards the desired result with the least possible guidance.Modular steps. You don’t have to run either plugin end-to-end, as both provide multiple skills that can be used in tandem or in isolation.Strict input and output schemas. Every step takes and returns a defined schema that includes the claim, the code revision, the required check, the raw evidence, and open questions. Fixed schemas reduce variability across runs and allow each step to verify the previous step’s work rather than trusting its summary.A live proof of concept for every claim. Every conclusion depends on a PoC run against a live deployment: a built, running instance of the project, reached through the interfaces a real user would use. When reproducing a bug, proving a fix, and confirming a regression, if a step can’t produce a live PoC, its result is inconclusive.regression-hunt reduces false positive ratesThe regression-hunt plugin (Figure 2):Enumerates candidate regressions by tracing the changed code (the diff) through its callers to its real interfaces.Reproduces each candidate regression on a live deployment of the system.Replays the PoC on the live deployment on a fresh-context agent.Judges the results of all the previous steps to validate that the proof meets the requirements of a regression.Figure 2: The regression-hunt workflow.
